Introduction
Synopsys Regression Debug Automation (RDA) is a solution that uses machine learning,
AI, and auto-trace technology to automate regression debug tasks. RDA automatically
groups failure cases (binning), finds root causes, and traces errors. It is designed for
complex System-on-Chip (SoC) and IP designs. Traditional regression debug flows need
engineers to spend a lot of time on manual binning, triaging, debugging, and tracing.
These tasks often start with many possible suspects and error points.
RDA automates the process of handling failed regression tests. It groups large numbers
of failed test cases, finds the root causes of failures, and identifies and isolates problem
areas. RDA also prepares debugging facilitators, completing these tasks much faster than
manual methods. By removing the need to compare waveforms, source code, and log files
manually, RDA reduces engineering effort and saves time--from days to just hours.

sorts and groups cases with the same failure type into one bucket.

RDA uses the Debug Facilitator to create the database and debugging environments
you need. This helps you debug each binning bucket in different debug modes.
Debug Facilitator uses a build script and a run-simulation script to rebuild and
rerun simulations after regression. This speeds up the process by reducing manual
preparation efforts. Furthermore, you can use the same scripts for future regressions.
Debug Facilitator includes reverse debug in interactive mode. This feature allows
you to control simulation execution both forward and backward. You can also enable
transaction recording to debug at the protocol level.
* DUT Root Cause Analysis

section: RDA provides a DUT Root Cause Analysis (DUTRCA) solution. This feature compares
text:
RDA provides a DUT Root Cause Analysis (DUTRCA) solution. This feature compares
a failed simulation with a previously passed simulation. It analyzes all suspect points
that might lead to regression failure and helps find the possible root causes. DUTRCA
automatically identifies and analyzes the possible causes by tracing back all error
points at the same time.
* Testbench Root Cause Analysis
RDA provides a Testbench Root Cause Analysis (TBRCA) solution that identifies the
testbench component with which the error is associated. It also identifies the region
within that component where the error is located.
The TBRCA Transaction Difference analysis flow analyzes and compares the reference
simulation log file with the failing simulation log file. It identifies the differences between
the transactions recorded during both simulations. The TBRCA Message Analysis
flow analyzes a message and identifies transactions and signals associated with that
message. Automatic detection of transaction differences helps you debug testbench
errors faster. This feature saves time during the debugging process.
* X Root Cause Analysis
All unknown X signals are automatically scanned and traced to their root causes. This
process saves manual effort. By managing and tracing many X signals automatically,
you spend less time repeating the same debugging steps.
* Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis

feature automatically groups violations detected by VCS-SDC into fewer groups. It

Overview
The first step after a regression failure is to process many failed cases. Manually checking,
analyzing, and organizing these cases can be very time-consuming and requires
significant manual work.
RDA offers Regression Binning, an automated process that uses machine learning and
data mining techniques to analyze failures and group those with the same issue type
together. The automation reduces engineer manual efforts and saves time.

Regression Binning Application
The Regression Binning application is an easy setup suitable for the Universal Verification
Methodology (UVM) regression environment and the SoC/IP level designs. Regression
Binning provides the following key features:
* Categorizes the simulation log files into different buckets, where each bucket
represents a failure type.
* Requires only simulation log files of the failed test cases.
* Provides a specific solution for the UVM-based error messages using unsupervised
machine learning based algorithm.
The Regression Binning application also supports the following advanced binning features:
* Extend binning capability by the user-defined rule of errors.
* Waive specific error patterns for binning.
* Group failed test cases without error messages but with a customized pass pattern,
recognized as Pass by RDA, in a Pass bucket.
* Replace or remove the unwanted parts of the specific error patterns.

<engine> command to auto generate an easy and ready-to-go template configuration
file, %> autorca -gen_cfg_template binning.yaml -gen_mode binning

3. This step is optional. Single-error binning uses a machine learning algorithm that

Configuring Database in the Configuration File
To enable Assigning and Managing Bucket feature, you must add Database setting in the
YAML configuration file. Add the following details in the Regression Binning configuration
file:
environment:
db_connection:
db_uri: sqlite@<file_path>
db_name: <db_name>
project_name: <proj_name>

Where,
* sqlite is an option for database.
* <file_path> is the location where the database is saved.
* <proj_name> is the unique name to save binning results in the same database file.
For example,
environment:
db_connection:
db_uri: sqlite@result.sqlite
db_name: test
project_name: test

Run the following commands to enable regression binning with database:
%> autorca -cfg run.yaml -create_db
%> autorca -cfg run.yaml
%> autorca -cfg run.yaml -show_report

Multiple-Error Binning
Multiple-error binning is based on the Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm to
calculate the similarities among the failed simulation logs. The simulation logs with similar
error message distributions are grouped into the same bucket using the Multiple-Error
Binning feature.
For example, a log file containing two UVM errors and one assertion error differs from a
log file containing only one UVM error. Even when both the log files have the same UVM
error, the two log files are grouped into different buckets.
The Multiple-Error Binning feature works in the following way:
* Collects all the error messages for each log file.
* Calculates the error distribution of each log file with the NLP algorithm based on all the
errors available in the logs.
* Groups log files into buckets with the error distribution of each log file.
Executing Multiple-Error Binning
By default, the machine learning single-error similarity binning is enabled. To enable
machine learning multiple-error binning, set the following option to true when you run
autorca -cfg run.yaml:
multiple_error_binning: true

By default, the multiple_error_binning option is set to false. After you enable the
multiple-error binning feature, run regression binning and load the report in the RCA
Manager.
In the RCA Manager, the Error Message section groups error message distributions in
each bucket. This section displays only the message part of the error message and the
error distribution of each log file. Variant parts of the messages are replaced with <*>.

RDA performs Regression Binning based on the predefined errors that include UVM
Errors, OVM Errors, SVA failures, Unsatisfied SystemVerilog constraints, and VCS
predefined errors.
However, when user-defined error messages in log files do not match predefined errors, or
when predefined errors do not meet the needs of your custom binning policy, Regression
Binning allows you to define your own rules. This feature allows Regression Binning to
operate according to your customized rules.
Add the required rules in a file, and specify the file in the user_defined_rule field of the
Regression Binning configuration file. To extend the Regression Binning capability, the
customizable rules are as follows:
* Waive rule: When you find negligible errors, you can specify the error patterns in the
Waive Rule, and then Regression Binning waives them from binning.
* User-defined errors rule:If your log files contain error messages that are not
predefined, specify the error patterns in the User-defined Errors Rule. Regression
Binning then considers these patterns as error messages.
* Pass rule: For the tests listed in the regression list without any error messages, you
can instruct Regression Binning to mark specific messages as pass tests.
* Replace rule: If failed tests fall into different groups based on error messages that
you consider the same, use the Replace Rule to remove or replace unwanted parts of
specific error patterns. Regression Binning uses the replaced error message to perform
similarity checking.
The following figure shows an example for the syntax of user_defined_rule. It consists
of two types of basic blocks, Filter and Waive, representing the specific error pattern to be
considered or waived.

1. Waive rule

Regression Binning With User-Defined Rules
The following steps describe how Regression Binning works with the user-defined rules:
* For each regression fail log, Regression Binning engine adopts waive rules to filter out
error messages that you want to ignore.
* Regression Binning engine adopts machine-learning based algorithm to classify the
target error message. It identifies all error messages that match the predefined and
user-defined error rules and follows the following criteria:
 When all errors have the same priority, the first identified error message is the target
error message.
 When errors have different priorities, the error message with the highest priority is
the target error message.
 When errors have different priorities and the error message with the highest priority
matches both, a predefined error rule and a user-defined error rule with the same
priority, the error message is still the target error message, and the predefined error
rule is applied.
When the predefined and user-defined errors are not found and the message matches
with any pass rules, the test case categorizes into a Pass bucket.

Priority Rules
The following priority rules are defined for several conditions:
* A lower priority value means higher priority. If you do not set a priority, the default
priority number for the predefined and user-defined error message is 1.
* If multiple error messages have the same priority, Regression Binning selects the first

priority, the predefined error rule overrides the user-defined error rule.

Regression Binning With Pass Rules
Test cases that do not show any error messages and where the simulation stops without
errors are placed in unknown buckets.
Regression Binning considers these test cases as passed tests by adding a Pass rule with
specific pass patterns. Tests that match this rule are binned into Pass buckets. All other
cases that do not match are binned into unknown buckets.

testcase= [case1][, case2]...//optional
desc= [descriptions1] //optional

Regression Binning With Replace Rules
When you have different error messages of the same kind or of the same error group, use
Replace rule. This rule informs Regression Binning to preprocess in the background and
replace the error messages.
Regression Binning preprocesses the line of error message with the replacement patterns.
It then uses the new replaced error message to perform similarity checking and binning.
Syntax:
replace_src=/<replace source >/
replace_dest=/<replace destination>/
desc=[replace description]

For example:
replace_src=/__VC\d+\//
replace_dest=/\//
desc=replace config pattern

Regression Binning replaces the replace_source pattern in the error message with the
replace_destination pattern and returns a new error message for binning.
If there are multiple replace_source patterns, the patterns are applied in the order they
appear in the user-defined rule file.

Overview
After regression, traditional debugging needs manual steps, such as rebuilding designs for
executable files that are deleted after regression. You also need to rerun simulations and
create Fast Signal Database (FSDB) files. Debugging is then performed in Verdi, either in
post-processing or interactive mode. For each failed test case, you must run the simulation
for the specific test pattern again. This process takes a lot of time.
RDA offers a solution for users who use Verdi VMS as their regression system. This
solution integrates Debug Facilitator with Verdi VMS. The integration uses Verdi VMS
configurations to perform Regression Binning (refer to the Regression Binning chapter for
more details). It facilitates the required database and debugging environments needed to
debug each bucket in different modes in Verdi.
After you add the RDA environment variables to the Verdi VMS .emc configuration file,
Debug Facilitator and Verdi VMS integrate directly. This integration rebuilds and reruns
simulations after regression runs in Verdi VMS. This integration makes the process faster.
It reduces the need to prepare scripts manually and removes the manual steps needed to
rerun simulations for each error case.

This chapter consists of the following sections:

Overview
After regression, traditional debugging needs manual steps, such as rebuilding designs for
executable files that are deleted after regression. You also need to rerun simulations and
create Fast Signal Database (FSDB) files. Debugging is then performed in Verdi, either in
post-processing or interactive mode. For each failed test case, you must run the simulation
for the specific test pattern again. This process takes a lot of time.
RDA provides Debug Facilitator to simplify the process. Debug Facilitator performs
Regression Binning (refer to the Regression Binning chapter for more details) and
facilitates the required database and debugging environments for debugging each binning
bucket in different modes in Verdi.
Debug Facilitator uses build and run-simulation scripts to rebuild and rerun simulations
after regression. This speeds up the process and reduces manual effort and time required
to perform the simulation for each error case. You can reuse these scripts for future
regressions.

text:
DUT Root Cause Analysis (DUTRCA)
This chapter consists of the following sections:
* Overview
* Technology Overview
* DUTRCA Application
* DUTRCA Usage
* Low-Power Debug for DUTRCA

Overview
Traditionally, comparing a failed test case in regression with a passed test case from a
previous regression takes a lot of time. This process includes checking waveforms, log
files, and source code. The reasons for a test case to fail might include changes in RTL,
enabling Xprop, changes in testbench, or any simulation migration. In complex designs,
finding where to start debugging and locating the root cause requires much manual work
and can be very time-consuming
RDA provides a DUT Root Cause Analysis (DUTRCA) solution. It automatically compares
a currently failed simulation with a previously passed simulation. It analyzes all suspect
points that could have caused the regression to fail and finds the possible root causes.

section: Using DUTRCA, Verdi automatically traces and compares the previously passed and
text:
Using DUTRCA, Verdi automatically traces and compares the previously passed and
currently failed designs and waveforms. It traces all error points together to help you find
and analyze possible root causes of the failure.
DUTRCA automation helps you find out why a simulation that passed before is now failing.
It does this by automatically searching for possible root causes using design changes and
both passing and failing FSDB files.

section: Overview of DUT Root Cause Analysis
text:
Overview of DUT Root Cause Analysis

After DUTRCA analysis, RDA provides the Verdi GUI that includes several debugging
tools. You can use these tools to review the analysis results, as well as the loaded design
and simulation results.
The DUTRCA solution helps you quickly find the root cause of failures. It automatically
analyzes differences between designs and simulation results. With DUTRCA, you do not
need to compare waveforms, source code, or log files manually. This saves engineering
time and effort, reducing debug time from days to hours.

section: Overview of DUT Root Cause Analysis
text:
Technology Overview
DUTRCA uses Simulation Failure Analyzer, Design Change Analyzer, and TraceDiff to
review the failed simulation log file. It uses reference KDB and FSDB files and target KDB
and FSDB files to automatically find the root cause due to design changes.
DUTRCA analyzes the log file to find the debug entries. It then compares these entries
in the waveform with the reference model to find signals with value differences. DUTRCA
traces how the difference signals move through the design. It then matches these signals
to the points where the design has changed.
Additionally, you can specify particular signals or scopes that need tracing, such as those
with errors. DUTRCA also helps trace differences when migrating to a new VCS version or
changing VCS options.

section: The key engines of DUTRCA are as follows:
text:
The key engines of DUTRCA are as follows:
* Log analysis: DUTRCA uses log analysis to automatically analyze log files and
get debug entries to trace the root cause. Log Analysis includes the following three
technologies to perform error message analysis:
 Assertion fail analysis: It detects the first assertion error message in the
simulation log file. It then uses the signals related to the assertion property as
debug entries, ensuring high accuracy.
 Signal match: It takes the key name from a UVM error or a user-defined error
message. It then maps with the tree-top design hierarchy. If the user-defined error
messages have high correlation with the design scope name, it finds the possible
candidate for the debug entry scope.
 Message analysis: It identifies the scoreboard that printed the message based on
the UVM error message. It then identifies the interface suitable for the debug entry
using the transaction dump information.
* Design difference analysis: DUTRCA automatically compares two simv.daidir files
and finds design changes between the two versions of the source codes. Additionally,

section: DUTRCA traces the root-causes based on the comparison and results.
text:
DUTRCA traces the root-causes based on the comparison and results.
* Waveform compare and value difference tracing: Through the Waveform
Comparison technology of Verdi nCompare, DUTRCA compares different types of
simulation results at different design phases. It uses the Waveform Value Difference
Tracing technology to trace back all caught error ports and identify and analyze the
possible root causes simultaneously.

Signal Match for Correlative Root Causes
After the root cause is sorted based on the waveform similarity analysis, signal match is
used to correlate root causes with the simulation log. Signal match identifies whether the
signal name relates to an error log. If the signal name relates to an error log, then that
signal name is listed at the highest rank in sorting.
Considering the root cause and its debug entries as a group, the related score can also
be calculated on the debug entry signal and root cause signal. It uses the highest score as
the root cause score. If a root cause is identified as a Correlative root cause, then it gets
the highest rank in sorting.

Overview
In a complex design environment, you construct the testbench with different components.
When an error occurs in a testbench component, finding the root cause can be difficult
and time-consuming. Testbench RCA identifies the root cause of testbench errors.
This includes identifying the specific testbench component and the region within that

When you introduce an error into a design environment, the error can occur in the DUT

identify the root cause, Testbench RCA reports these as "items of interest" to help you to
debug.
If a design that was previously operating correctly begins to fail, it can be challenging

entire environment. Further, the error might not be reported at the simulation time where
the error occurs. You might not be able to detect and report the error immediately during

Transaction Difference Analysis
The TBRCA Transaction Difference Analysis flow analyzes two FSDB files - one from a
passing case and another from a related failing case. It identifies the differences between
the transactions recorded in two simulations. You can view and analyze the resulting
transaction differences and associated interface signals in the Verdi GUI.
The following are the requirements for Target and Reference Simulations and FSDB:
* Enable recording of all items associated with the UVM or OVM testbench.
* Use the same seed for both the passing and failing test cases. This avoids transaction
or sequence differences related to randomization.

Transaction Difference Analysis Flow

The Transaction Difference Analysis flow consists of the following major operations:
1. Interface analysis: The interface signals in both the passing and failing test cases are
analyzed and compared. These signals connect the testbench with the RTL code. For
more details on interface analysis, refer to Interface Analysis.
2. UVM/OVM characteristics analysis: The UVM or OVM hierarchy is compared
between the passing and failing designs. This comparison checks the basic structure
of the hierarchy, that includes comparing the number of components and their
connections. It also looks at activity of certain operations associated with the hierarchy,
such as when objections are raised and lowered. For more details on UVM/OVM
characteristics analysis, refer to UVM/OVM Characteristics Analysis.
3. Transaction comparison: Transactions recorded during the simulation of the passing
and failing tests are compared. The UVM or OVM transactions are compared. If the
design includes Synopsys VIPs that support Protocol Analyzer, these transactions are
compared and reported separately. For more details on transaction comparison, refer
to Transaction Comparison.
4. Debugging in Verdi GUI: You can view and analyze the results of comparing passing
and failing tests in the Verdi environment. Use the following command: autorca
-load_report <report_path>. For more details on debugging in Verdi GUI, refer to
Debugging in Verdi GUI.
Message Analysis is used only when the differences are not found between transactions in
the passing and failing tests. TBRCA uses message analysis to identify transactions that
might be related to the first error message. This helps in debugging the error.

Interface Analysis
Interface analysis determines which signal on the testbench/RTL boundary is the first
to differ and in which direction. When the UVM/OVM information is recorded during
simulation, details about the interfaces that are connected to the testbench are also
recorded. These interfaces are analyzed by TBRCA.

Scenarios to Perform Interface Analysis
You can come across the following scenarios while performing interface analysis:
1. When you find differences while comparing interface signals, first determine the
direction of each signal. TBRCA attempts to identify whether the interface signal is
driven by RTL code or by testbench code.
Note:
As SystemVerilog interface signals do not have an explicit direction
associated with them, TBRCA analyzes the SystemVerilog source code to
determine the direction.
2. When the first difference involves an interface signal driven from the RTL to the
testbench, the error likely exists in the RTL code (DUT). When the first difference is
associated with an interface signal driven from the testbench to the RTL, the error likely
exists in the testbench code.
3. When you find no differences while comparing the interface signals, but an error still
occurs, the error most likely exists in an internal testbench component.
4. When differences appear in both testbench inputs and outputs, and the first differences
occur at the same time, the error might exist in the DUT or the testbench. This situation
occurs because a feedback loop connects the testbench code and the RTL code.

section: The Testbench RCA Message Analysis flow analyzes messages using a Natural
text:
The Testbench RCA Message Analysis flow analyzes messages using a Natural
Language Processing (NLP) algorithm. It identifies transactions and signals closely
associated with that message. The resulting transactions and signals can then be
analyzed in the Verdi GUI.
The message to be analyzed can be selected based on the options specified to TBRCA.

analysis algorithm identifies transactions linked to a message. It parses and analyzes the

Analyzing Log Message From the Extracted Log File
The simulation log file contains different types of log messages, and you can extract the
types of log messages needed for analysis into a separate file, as shown in the following

In the YAML configuration file, you can input the extracted log file to be analyzed using the
analyze_extract_msg_file option. This is shown in the following figure:
Figure 134

Analyzing the Extracted Message File

TBRCA always picks the first valid log message irrespective of the type (Fatal, Error,
Warning, or Information) from the extracted file for analysis. If the first character of a line
contains #, assuming it to be a comment, TBRCA picks the next line.
The extracted log file must contain the line number and its associated log message.
TBRCA considers colon (:) as a delimiter to differentiate line number and log message at
each line. It takes the left hand side of the colon as the line number of the log message
and the right-hand side of the colon as the log message.

In the YAML configuration file, the target_sim_log option is mandatory
and you must specify the original log file from which the log messages are

Time Out Related Cases Support
Simulation can be timed out with or without generating a UVM_ERROR. When the
simulation generates a UVM_ERROR even after it is timed out, analyzing UVM_ERROR is
not useful. Therefore, Message Analysis provides a solution of collecting thread details to
analyze the time-out related cases.

Collecting Thread Details
To collect the thread details, you must set the time-out time when the simulation stops
responding and update the VCS runtime arguments.
Setting time-out time
To collect the thread details at a particular time, set the simulation time-out or the time
when the simulation stops responding using the following environment variable:
setenv TBRCA_COLLECT_THREAD_TIME <simulation time>

For example, setenv TBRCA_COLLECT_THREAD_TIME 20000
Consider a simulation that runs from time 0 to 100000 and the time-out starts from the
time 20000, then you can set any time between 20000 to 100000 to collect the thread
details. The time-out value helps Message Analysis to stop simulation at the given time
and collect the thread details.

Updating VCS Runtime Arguments
In addition to the setting time-out, you can also add the following VCS runtime arguments
to collect the required details:
-ucli -i <$VERDI_HOME>/etc/tbAutoRCA/scripts/log_analysis/analyzers/
tbrca_timeout_analysis.tcl

After the simulation is completed, Message Analysis collects all the active thread details
which include Running, Waiting, and Blocking.
You can run the Message Analysis and open the report to view, navigate, and search the
thread details to identify the suspicious thread causing the simulation time-out.

X Root Cause Analysis (XRCA)
This chapter consists of the following sections:
* Overview
* What is XRCA?
* XRCA Application
* XRCA Usage
* XRCA Root Cause Reasons

Overview
Traditionally, unknown values (Xs) typically propagate through the design over multiple
statements. There are many root causes of unknown values. For example, if there is an
X in the input of a logic gate, if memory is not initialized, or if there is a setup or hold time
violation.
Usually, multiple Xs occur together. When you have multiple unknowns, select one X as
the startpoint for debugging, even if it is in your log or signal list. Then, trace backward
through the driver or fan-in signals of your chosen signal until you find the earliest X. If
the signal you selected is not the only cause of unknowns, pick another X from the group
and repeat the process. This cycle involves several small, repeated steps that can be
organized and automated.
XRCA automatically scans X signals in FSDB files and traces each X signal to its root
cause. It can process many X signals together, which reduces debugging time. XRCA also
creates clear, organized reports of the root causes. You can load these reports in Verdi to
view the tracing paths.
XRCA is a useful tool for debugging X signals during the start of gate-level simulation
and for finding X signal issues during regression. XRCA supports tracing at the gatelevel netlist, RTL, and VCS X propagation. It also helps trace X signals from low power
components and can detect X-pessimism.

Verdi(R) Regression Debug Automation (RDA) User Guide
Y-2026.03-SP2

What is XRCA?
XRCA is a highly effective tool that helps you quickly trace the path from an unknown
signal at an observation point to the root cause signal. This saves significant manual effort.
Using the input design and FSDB, XRCA with the tracing technology automatically traces
groups of X signals to their root causes. It also has built-in knowledge of how X values are
generated. With the analyzing technology, XRCA analyzes the root causes and generates
categorized reports. These reports are text files, and you can also use the capability for
further debugging in Verdi Apex mode. After the design and FSDB are ready, all tracings
and analysis steps run automatically, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 150

Figure 151 shows that XRCA uses the dumped waveform and design as inputs. You
can also specify a signal list to only focus on specific signals with X values. If you do not
provide a signal list, XRCA runs in auto-scan mode. In auto-scan mode, it scans and
traverses all signals of the FSDB and generates a list of signals with X values.

XRCA helps you find out the root causes of X signals. However, some X signals might be
false alarms due to X-pessimism. To identify X, you need to check the false X manually.
This is a time-consuming process.

If A has an unknown value, the simulation value of the AND gate is X. However, you can
find out that the result of an AND gate must be 0 because A AND  is always equal to 0
(zero), irrespective of the value of A.

XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
XRCA automatically identifies cases where an X root cause is driven by a timing violation
reported in the simulation log. After running XRCA, a post-processing module performs the
following tasks:
* Scans XRCA root causes.
* Correlates them with timingviolation messages in the simulation log (VCS or thirdparty formats).
* Annotates matching root causes as timing violation and records the exact
simulation log file and line in the XRCA report.
When you load xrca_report.xml,
* For root causes that correlate to a timing violation, XRCA updates the displayed reason
text to X from timing violation.
* When a timingviolation subsection is present for a root cause, the GUI adds a
timing violation tree widget under that root cause.
* Use Show Timing Violation on SmartLog in SmartLog to open the simulation log
and jump to the recorded line. Use Show Timing Violation on Source View in
Source View to navigate to the related source location.

Enabling XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
The XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation feature is conditionally enabled. To use this
feature, all of the following must be true:
* The timing_violation_check option is enabled in the XRCA YAML template.
* A valid simulation log path, target_sim_log, is specified in the XRCA YAML template.
* The file at that path exists and can be opened for reading.
However, if timing_violation_check is set to false, if the target_sim_log field is
missing or empty, or if the simulation log file cannot be opened, then
* The timing-violation post process is skipped.
* No timing-violation annotation is applied.
* No change to root cause reasons.
* No additional navigation is enabled.

Post-Processing After XRCA Run
After the XRCA run completes, the tool performs the following postprocessing steps to
correlate root causes with timing violations:
1. Extracts root-cause information from the XRCA output
a. After XRCA finishes, the output file xrca_report.xml is available.
b. XRCA parses xrca_report.xml to identify all <rootCause> entries.
c. For each root cause, the tool extracts the full signal name and identifies the driven
scope instance. The tool considers cross-module references (XMRs) also.
d. XRCA builds an inmemory list of root-cause signals and scopes, to be used in
subsequent searches.
2. Correlates root causes with timing violations in the simulation log
a. The tool uses the root-cause list and the specified simulation-log file
(target_sim_log).
b. It searches the simulation log for candidate locations that match a root-cause
scope.
c. When several timing-violation candidates exist, the tool selects the violation with a
time closest to, but earlier than, the original root-cause time.
d. For each candidate location, the tool checks whether it forms a valid
timingviolation block, based on existing SmartLog rules.

Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis

This chapter consists of the following sections:
* Overview

Overview
During RTL simulation, Dynamic SDC Verification in VCS detects timing constraint bugs,
such as Multiple Cycle Path (MCP), FP, and clock group issues. SDC forms a key part of
RTL signoff. Teams use VCS with SDC (VCS-SDC) for signoff during verification. VCSSDC reduces project cycle time by several weeks.
Debugging violations detected by VCS-SDC can be difficult when MCP bugs affect many
signals. RDA offers a Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis (MCPRCA) solution. This
solution automatically groups violations into fewer categories. It provides connections to
further debug with waveform, source code, and simulation log, using Verdi.

text:
MCPRCA helps you to debug the VCS-SDC detected violations using Verdi. After
completing simulation with VCS-SDC, MCPRCA checks the results of VCS-SDC and
helps in finding out the violations. MCPRCA uses the Violation Binning feature to group
violations from a simulation log and generate further debug entries.

text:
RDA provides the Verdi GUI to review MCPRCA reports generated after analyzing
violations from the log file. You can also use the GUI to debug the source code, logs, and
waveform.

You can use the Smart Waiver feature to reduce noise by removing the violation indexes

name, the FROM signal and the TO signal.

Waive violation index matches FROM signal and TO signal. Signal name is allowed to use
wildcard (* ?)
* waive -name $RuleName -to {<$ToSignalName>} -from {<$FromSignalName>}
To disable waive rule, rule names are separated with a space.

text:
General Fault Analysis
Debugging general faults, such as NO, NN, ND, and so on, means that you need to
trace the fanout from the fault location. Follow the path finding the blocking points in the
downstream circuits until you reach an observation or detection point. This is a timeconsuming process that requires manual efforts.
To overcome the limitation of excessive manual effort and time consumption, FaultRCA
provides utility that helps in detecting the blocking points between the fault-injected point
and the observation or detection point.
A path is created from the fault location to the observation point. Along this path, you can
identify and collect blocking points. This helps you focus on the path and attempt to make
the fault move from the injected point) to the observation point.

chapter: Chapter 9: Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis (MCPRCA)
text:
Blocking Points
Blocking points are the points through which a fault cannot propagate. For example, as
shown in Figure 209, assume A is the fault location where the fault SA1 (stuck-at-1) is
injected. The fault propagates to C. However, the fault cannot propagate to D.
As the value of B is constantly 0, the primitive AND gate never allows the fault at C to
propagate to D. Because the fault is not propagated to D, the AND cell is called the
blocking cell.

Verdi(R) Regression Debug Automation (RDA) User Guide

Fault Analysis Method
The fault analysis method provides the following two modes:
* Static Trace Mode
* Block Cell Detection Mode

Static Trace Mode
FaultRCA traces the path from the input fault to the destination point. You can either
extract the observation point from the fault database (FDB) or provide a list of signals to
the tool. You can run this mode in the following two ways:
* Target Signal Mode
* Auto Mode

Target Signal Mode
To analyze one or more signals, use target signal mode. In this mode, you must provide
one or multiple input signals. The information, such as observations list and signal type,
are extracted from the FDB. FaultRCA generates an XML report (.xml) and a text report
(.txt) containing the tracing path.

Verdi(R) Regression Debug Automation (RDA) User Guide
Y-2026.03-SP2

232

General Fault Analysis

Feedback

The format of the fault list file is <Signal Full hierarchy name>. For example,
top.a.b
top.c.d.e

Auto Mode
To analyze a list of critical location points available in the FDB, use auto mode. Auto
mode analyzes more than one signal, and it allows you to select the number of signals to
analyze. The FaultRCA utility automatically analyzes the most critical locations, that is, the
blocking points that cover highest number of NO fault from the FDB. It generates an XML
report and a text report containing tracing paths of all the signals. The information, such as
observation points, signal types, and a list of critical blocking points is extracted from the
FDB.

Block Cell Detection Mode
FaultRCA traces a path between the input fault to the destination point and finds any
blocking cell along the path. You can get the observation point from the FDB or provide
a list of signals to the tool. For this mode, you need the dumped waveform from either a
good machine or faulty machine (gm/fm). One input pin has the GM/FM annotation value.
All output pins have only the GM annotation values.
A block instance on a flip-flop checks the current status of the GM/FM annotation and the
incoming clock cycle. Specifically, it checks the input GM/FM status in the current clock
cycle and the output GM/FM status in the next clock cycle.
When the next clock cycle arrives at the signal connected to the register clock port, the
block checks the clock port. If the clock port is rising or falling, it finds the next rising or
falling time. Otherwise, it finds the next time the value changes.
This mode supports only Stuck@0 and Stuck@1. You can run it in the target signal mode.

Target Signal Mode
If you want to analyze one or multiple signals, use target signal mode. In this mode, you
must provide one or multiple input signals and the target signal list name.
The following is the format of the fault list:
<stuck@0>/<stuck@1>, <Signal full hierarchy name>

For example,
0, top.a.b
1, top.c.d.e

Running Fault Analysis
You can run fault analysis using autorca in the static trace mode and the block cell
detection mode.
To generate the configuration file template (run.yaml), use the following command:
autorca -gen_cfg_template <run.yaml> -gen_mode faultrca

When you run the command, the run.yaml file is generated.

Requirements
The following are the requirements to run fault analysis:
* The simv.daidir directory
* The mode field must be set to 1 by default.
* The gm/fm waveform is required for the block cell detection mode.
For FDB, you must specify the following fields:
* FDB project name: Specify the name of the FDB project to be used.
* FDB path: Specify the full path of the FDB directory.
* Campaign name: Specify the campaign name that is used for dumping FDB.
* For the destination point, you can provide the text file or extract the observation or
detection point from the FDB.
For the target signal mode, you must specify the text file containing the name of the
signals. For more information on the format of the fault list file for the static trace mode
and the block cell detection mode, refer to the Static Trace Mode and Block Cell Detection
Mode sections, respectively.
For the auto mode, specify the number of top critical locations that you require.

NC Analysis
The Not Controllable (NC) analysis provides a method to reduce manual efforts while
cleaning up the NC faults. NC faults occur in unselected signals during fault simulation.
An NC fault happens when the fanin value stays constant, which makes the fault
uncontrollable.
The existing FDB consists of multiple critical locations, and each critical location consists
of multiple faults. The faults are categorized with common location points to determine
which location point has the maximum number of NC faults. To find the root cause, you
must trace through the NC locations to find the faults where the fanin value remains
constant. This is a time-consuming process.
The NC analysis automates tracing and scans for every NC location, and traces its fanin
cone. The tracing continues until no fanin or all fanin are found with the changed values.
This ensures that the root cause is found. The root cause with the highest number of
critical locations and faults is the top root cause. The report displays the root-cause bucket
containing all the root causes, critical locations, and faults grouped inside the blocking
points.
NC Faults
NC faults are faults that stay constant during simulation. These faults occur when a signal,
which is the input to the fault, does not change its value. That is, the value stays at zero
or one throughout the simulation. The 0-X-0 or 1-X-1 state does not count as switching
states. You must run the fault manager with testability enabled to generate NC faults. The

Fault Ranking
The Fault Ranking utility automates to streamline debugging efforts. It focuses on blocking
points in the FDB that are caused from the same root cause, where the value does not
change. The automation reduces the redundant debugging.
The NC Fault Ranking utility scans all the critical locations with NC faults, It traces its fanin
cone until it finds no fanin or all fanin pins with changed values. In the NC Fault Ranking
report, a signal with no fanin or all fanin pins with the changed values is categorized as the
NC root cause. Critical locations are grouped based on the same root cause. The FDB NC
faults are grouped by the same critical location, and the critical locations are grouped by
the same root cause. All root causes that are formed by the same signal and module are
grouped together.
This automation minimizes manual debugging and traces NC signals directly to their root
causes, saving significant time and effort.
